implementation_notes: In C++ a `goto` crossing a variable's initialisation is ill-formed, so the compiler already forbids the worst combinations; what remains is the long `try`/`catch` block used as a control structure (catch-all `catch(...)` that swallows and continues), and deeply nested conditionals inside large functions. The C++-specific remedy for the flag form is RAII plus an explicit state object: scope guards remove the ad-hoc cleanup flags that drive much C-family spaghetti. C++ Core Guidelines' ban on `goto` for backward jumps and on multiple `return`s in one function is the concrete local rule to cite in review.
idiom_name: goto plus RAII-interacting jumps; nested try/catch as control flow
pitfalls: `catch (...) { return; }` turns the exception mechanism into a goto and discards the reason the code failed.
Header-only template code can be control-flow-dense without being readable; template metaprogramming is a separate smell.
